prompt: Where does this course get the numbers it uses to answer "when will it be ready?"

choices.text: From a new survey the team fills in every week
choices.why: The course asks for no new data collection; a weekly survey is extra work and still an opinion.

choices.text: From the estimate of whoever is closest to the work
choices.why: That is the opinion the course replaces: given in good faith and wrong in the same direction.

choices.text: From industry benchmarks for teams of the same size
choices.why: Another team's numbers describe another system. The course measures this team's own history.

choices.text: From records the team already keeps
choices.why: Right. Start and finish dates, deployments and incidents are already recorded; the course reads them.

prompt: The Billing team changed its rules on 3 August. What does that do to the history from June and July as a basis for forecasting September?

choices.text: Nothing: more history is always a better basis for a forecast
choices.why: More history helps only while it describes the same system; June and July describe the old rules.

choices.text: It becomes useless for anything, including explaining the change
choices.why: It is exactly what shows what the change did; it stops describing the present, not the past.

choices.text: It describes a team that no longer works that way
choices.why: Right. A history describes the system that produced it, and that system changed on 3 August.

choices.text: It must be averaged with August so the two policies balance out
choices.why: An average of two policies describes neither of them; lesson 1's last section shows the result.

prompt: A team finishes 4 items a week and keeps 12 items in progress on an ordinary day. By Little's law, how many weeks does an item take on average?
A team has an average cycle time of 6 days and finishes 1.5 items a day. What is its average work in progress, in items?
A team finishing five items a week raises its open items from ten to twenty, and its throughput does not change. What happens to the average cycle time?

choices.text: It halves, because twice as much is being worked on
choices.why: Open is not the same as being worked on; with the same throughput the extra items wait.

choices.text: It stays the same, since nobody works more slowly
choices.why: Each item takes as much effort as before and spends longer waiting for its turn.

choices.text: It doubles, from two weeks to four
choices.why: Right. 10 ÷ 5 is two weeks and 20 ÷ 5 is four: more open work, same output, older work.

choices.text: It cannot be said without timing the items
choices.why: That is the point of the law: two averages give the third without timing anything.

prompt: Which of these does Little's law need to hold over the period you measure? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: What starts in the period eventually finishes
choices.why: Right. An abandoned or deleted item unbalances the books.

choices.text: Work in progress is about the same at both ends
choices.why: Right. A board that fills or empties is a ramp, not a system.

choices.text: Every item is about the same size
choices.why: The law is about averages; items can vary as much as they like.

choices.text: Throughput and cycle time use the same calendar
choices.why: Right. Per calendar day goes with calendar days; mixing them breaks the arithmetic.

choices.text: The team uses Kanban rather than Scrum
choices.why: It is a theorem about any queue: a bank, a router, a Scrum team.

prompt: A support team cuts its open tickets from 30 to 15, and its throughput falls from 10 a day to 5, because half the team now sits idle waiting for tickets. What does Little's law say happens to the average time a ticket takes?

choices.text: Nothing: 30 ÷ 10 and 15 ÷ 5 are both three days
choices.why: Right. Cutting work in progress shortens cycle time only while throughput holds; here it fell in proportion.

choices.text: It halves, because work in progress halved
choices.why: That holds only with throughput fixed, and here throughput halved too.

choices.text: It doubles, because the team is slower
choices.why: The team finishes less, but each ticket spends the same three days inside.

choices.text: The law stops applying when people are idle
choices.why: Idle people change throughput; the law still relates the three averages.

prompt: What does the course ask you to install to run its programs?

choices.text: Python 3, version 3.8 or newer, and nothing else
choices.why: Right. The standard library is enough, so there is nothing to install with pip.

choices.text: Python 3 and a set of libraries installed with pip
choices.why: No library is needed: every program uses only what comes with Python.

choices.text: A board tool with an account for the Billing team
choices.why: The team's history is written by a program you run; no tool or account is involved.

choices.text: A spreadsheet, because the programs are spreadsheet formulas
choices.why: The programs are Python; a spreadsheet can open the CSV files to look at them, and that is all.

prompt: On Windows with Python installed from python.org, what should you type wherever a lesson types python3?

choices.text: python2
choices.why: That would be the old Python, if it existed at all; the course needs 3.8 or newer.

choices.text: py
choices.why: Right. The python.org installer puts the py launcher on Windows.

choices.text: pip3
choices.why: pip installs packages; it does not run programs, and the course installs none.

choices.text: %%writefile
choices.why: That is a Colab cell command for saving a file, not a way to run Python.

prompt: Why does the course name two online services rather than one?

choices.text: Because each one runs only half of the programs
choices.why: Both run every program; they are alternatives, not halves.

choices.text: Because the lessons were recorded on both of them
choices.why: The lessons were recorded on a Linux computer, the installed path.

choices.text: So that no lesson depends on one company's terms
choices.why: Right. If one changes its terms, the other path, or the installed one, gives the same numbers.

choices.text: Because one is for Windows users and one for macOS users
choices.why: Both run in a browser on any system.

prompt: Why does your copy of items.csv come out byte for byte the same as the lesson's?

choices.text: Because the program downloads the file from the course
choices.why: Nothing is downloaded; the program writes the file on your computer.

choices.text: Because its random numbers come from a fixed seed
choices.why: Right. A random.Random with a fixed seed gives the same sequence on every computer, so the simulation repeats exactly.

choices.text: Because the history is typed into the program row by row
choices.why: The rows are simulated one day at a time, not written out.

choices.text: Because Python rounds every date to the same day
choices.why: Dates are not rounded; they come from the simulated days.

prompt: Match each column of items.csv to what it records.

pairs.right: the day the item entered the backlog
the day somebody started working on it
the day it was handed over for review
when its review finished and the change merged

prompt: Before 3 August the Billing team deployed every Thursday; after it, every working day. What does billing.py assume about a deployment that carries more changes?

choices.text: More likely to fail, and slower to undo when it fails
choices.why: Right. Both the failure chance and the repair time grow with the size of the batch.

choices.text: It is safer, because the changes were tested together
choices.why: The program assumes the opposite, and lessons 5 to 7 measure why.

choices.text: It fails as often as any other but is undone faster
choices.why: A bigger batch has more changes that can be wrong and more to untangle.

choices.text: Its size makes no difference to anything
choices.why: Size is exactly what the program uses for both the chance and the repair time.

prompt: billing.py ran from your home folder, printed its summary line, and your delivery folder still has no items.csv. Why?

choices.text: The program failed silently and wrote nothing
choices.why: It wrote both files; they are in the folder the terminal was in.

choices.text: Python needs administrator rights to write a CSV file
choices.why: No special rights are needed to write in your own folders.

choices.text: Files are written where you run it, not where it lives
choices.why: Right. The two CSV files are in the home folder; run everything from delivery.

choices.text: The summary line is printed before the files are written
choices.why: The print is the last line of the program, after both files are written.

prompt: Python reports IndentationError on a line of a program you pasted from the lesson. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: Your Python is too old for the program
choices.why: An old Python fails with a SyntaxError on the f-strings, not on indentation.

choices.text: The paste lost spaces at the start of a line
choices.why: Right. Python reads those spaces as structure; copy with the block's button into a plain text editor.

choices.text: The file was saved in a different folder from items.csv
choices.why: A file in the wrong folder gives "can't open file", before any line is read.

choices.text: The data in items.csv is malformed
choices.why: Indentation is checked before the program runs, long before it opens a file.

prompt: In August the Billing team averaged 10.5 items in progress and finished 1.32 items a day. What cycle time does Little's law predict, in days, to one decimal place?
In September the law predicts 6.0 days and the finished items averaged 5.0. What explains the gap?

choices.text: Weekends are counted in work in progress but not in cycle time
choices.why: Both count calendar days in littles.py, so the units agree.

choices.text: Little's law only holds approximately for teams of people
choices.why: It is a theorem; the gap had a cause, and removing the cause closes it.

choices.text: The team started limiting work in progress in September
choices.why: The limit started on 3 August; September was the first whole month under it.

choices.text: One item stayed open all month, blocked
choices.why: Right. BIL-189 adds one to every day's count and nothing to any cycle time; without it the two agree.

prompt: Run littles.py for June and July and the law predicts 25.3 days while the finished items averaged 19.1. Which reading is right?
hint: Look at what was still open on 31 July, and when it finished.

choices.text: The team was faster in June and July than the law allows a team to be
choices.why: No team beats a theorem; the measurement left something out.

choices.text: The old rules made Little's law stop applying
choices.why: The law applies to any rules; what failed was a condition of the measurement.

choices.text: The window missed late finishes of items open on 31 July
choices.why: Right. Twenty-six items were open on 31 July; their waiting is in July's work in progress and their cycle times land in August.

choices.text: The program counts work in progress wrongly before the rules changed
choices.why: It counts the same way every day; the window's edges are the problem.

prompt: Over all four months the law and the measurement agree within a day. Why is that period still a poor one to quote?

choices.text: It blends two policies into averages that describe neither
choices.why: Right. 14.9 items in progress, when the team carried about 22 in June and July and 6 in September.

choices.text: Four months is too short a window for Little's law to apply properly
choices.why: Agreement within a day shows the law holding; the problem is what the numbers describe.

choices.text: It includes weekends, which distort the throughput
choices.why: Every period here counts weekends the same way.

choices.text: It leaves out the items finished in August
choices.why: August is inside June to September.

prompt: Little's law, in a team's words: average work in progress equals throughput times average ___ time.
A team counts 21 items on its board this morning and finished 42 items in the last 28 days. Using Little's law, roughly how many days should a new item expect to take?
Put the steps of checking Little's law on a board in order.
items: Choose a period in which the team's rules did not change
Count the open items at the end of every day and average them
Divide the items finished in the period by its days
Divide average work in progress by throughput
Compare the result with the measured average cycle time

prompt: A manager wants items to finish sooner and proposes that each developer start one more item so that more is always moving. Throughput has been flat for months. What does the law predict?

choices.text: Items finish sooner, because more of them are in motion
choices.why: In motion is not finishing; the team's output is what it was.

choices.text: Items take longer, because the same output is shared by more open work
choices.why: Right. With throughput flat, adding work in progress raises the average cycle time in proportion.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the law ignores who works on what
choices.why: It ignores who, and it counts how many; how many is what the proposal changes.

choices.text: Throughput rises, because nobody is ever waiting for work
choices.why: Nobody was waiting for work before either; the queue in front of review is what grows.

prompt: What does a team learn when Little's law and its measured cycle time disagree badly over a period?

choices.text: That the board data is wrong and should be thrown away
choices.why: The data may be fine; the disagreement points at the system rather than at the records.

choices.text: That the team should switch to a different metric
choices.why: The disagreement is the useful finding; switching metrics would hide it.

choices.text: That the system changed during the period, or something open is not finishing
choices.why: Right. August was a change of rules; September's smaller gap was one blocked item.

choices.text: That the law needs a correction factor for software teams
choices.why: There is no correction factor; the conditions either hold or they do not.
